lead: Gaussian elimination is the working method behind every linear solver: use row operations to push zeros under each pivot until the augmented matrix is a staircase, then read the unknowns bottom-up. Gauss–Jordan keeps going, clearing above the pivots too, so the answers sit in the last column with no substitution. The recipe needs no matrix inverse and no guesswork, which is why it is used to solve circuit equations, fit curves to data, balance chemical reactions, and settle large systems inside engineering software.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for writing Ax = b, and 1.2 for the three row operations and the echelon staircase.

sections.h3: The elimination recipe: forward phase, then back substitution

blocks.text: Elimination on the augmented matrix [A|b] has two phases. The forward phase pushes zeros below each pivot and stops at staircase (echelon) form. The backward phase recovers the unknowns, either by substituting upward or by pushing zeros above the pivots too.
A pivot is the first non-zero number in a row after elimination; it is the number you divide by to get that unknown. The multiplier is the factor that kills the entry below a pivot.
a_ij ← a_ij − m·a_kj,  m = a_ik / a_kk
blocks.where: a_kk is the pivot in row k (never 0); a_ik is the entry in row i, column k, that must become 0; m is the multiplier; a_ij and a_kj are the column-j entries of rows i and k.

items: Write the system as [A|b]: coefficients on the left, constants in the last column.
Take the leftmost column with a non-zero entry at or below the current row. That entry is the pivot.
For each row i below the pivot: m = a_ik / a_kk, then R_i ← R_i − m·R_k. The entry a_ik becomes exactly 0.
Move down one row and right one column and repeat, until no further pivots appear. You now have echelon form.
Back substitute: solve the last pivot row for its single unknown, then work upward, putting known values into the row above.

blocks.text: Nothing is inverted, and each step is one division plus a few subtractions. Hand elimination on a 3 × 3 system is about a page of work. Used this way, the same three row operations from 1.2 carry the whole system to an answer.

sections.h3: Gauss–Jordan: clear above the pivot and read the answer

blocks.text: Gauss–Jordan deletes the backward phase by doing more work in the forward phase. It also clears the entries above each pivot, then scales the pivot to 1, so every pivot column looks like a column of the identity matrix.

items: Find the pivot in column k; swap rows if the entry there is 0.
Scale: R_k ← R_k / a_kk, so the pivot becomes 1.
Clear the whole column: for every other row i, R_i ← R_i − a_ik·R_k. Column k now holds 1 in row k and 0 in every other row.
Repeat for each pivot, working left to right.
The matrix is in reduced row echelon form (RREF) and x_k = b′_k is read straight from the last column, with no substitution.

blocks.text: The same reduction on [A|I] turns A into I, and the right block becomes A⁻¹; that is the standard hand method for inverses, and Unit 3 explains when the inverse exists. The price is arithmetic: about n³/2 multiplications against n³/3 for Gaussian elimination on an n × n system. Gauss–Jordan is easier to read on paper; production software prefers the cheaper triangular approach, which is the LU factorization of 1.5.

sections.h3: Zero pivots, skipped columns and free variables

blocks.text: A zero pivot is not a failure. Search column k at and below the current row for a non-zero entry, swap that row up, and continue. A row swap is a legal elementary row operation, so the solution set does not change.

If the whole pivot column at and below the current row is zero, no pivot can be made. Skip that column, move one column right, and finish the elimination. The unknown of a skipped column is not tied to any pivot: it is a free variable and may take any real value.

blocks.where: n is the number of unknowns (columns of A) and r is the number of pivots in the echelon form. If r = n there is one solution; if r < n there are infinitely many, written with parameters t₁, t₂, …; a row like [0 0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0 means no solution, as 1.4 develops.

blocks.text: Partial pivoting: always swap the entry of largest absolute value in the pivot column into the pivot position. Every multiplier then satisfies |m| ≤ 1, so entries do not blow up and rounding error stays small. Hand calculations also get easier, because the numbers stay small.

blocks.where: a_jk runs over the rows at and below the pivot row; choosing the largest one as the pivot keeps every multiplier at or below 1 in size.

figure.caption: Both branches begin from the same row reduction of [A|b]. The left branch stops at echelon form and back-substitutes; the right branch continues to reduced form and reads each unknown straight from the last column.

spec.aria: A decision tree: from the row reduction of the augmented matrix, one branch stops at echelon form and back-substitutes, the other continues to reduced form and reads the solution directly.

examples.question: Solve the system x + y + z = 3, 2x + 2y + 2z = 6, x − y = 0 by Gaussian elimination, and give the general solution with its free parameter.
steps: Write the augmented matrix: R1 = [1, 1, 1 | 3], R2 = [2, 2, 2 | 6], R3 = [1, −1, 0 | 0].
Pivot a₁₁ = 1. Multiplier for R2: m = 2/1 = 2. R2 ← R2 − 2R1 gives [0, 0, 0 | 0].
Multiplier for R3: m = 1/1 = 1. R3 ← R3 − R1 gives [0, −2, −1 | −3].
Swap the zero row to the bottom (R2 ↔ R3): [1, 1, 1 | 3], [0, −2, −1 | −3], [0, 0, 0 | 0].
Pivot in column 2 is −2. Scale R2 by −1/2: [0, 1, 1/2 | 3/2]. Echelon form reached.
Count: r = 2 pivots among n = 3 unknowns, so n − r = 1 free parameter. Column 3 has no pivot, so z is free: put z = t.
Back substitution, row 2: y + z/2 = 3/2, so y = (3 − t)/2. Row 1: x + y + z = 3, so x = 3 − (3 − t)/2 − t = (3 − t)/2.
examples.answer: General solution x = y = (3 − t)/2 and z = t for any real number t; at t = 1 the solution is (1, 1, 1).
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction as F

def sol(t):
    x = F(3 - t, 2)
    y = F(3 - t, 2)
    z = F(t)
    return x, y, z

for t in [F(0), F(1), F(5), F(1, 2)]:
    x, y, z = sol(t)
    assert x + y + z == 3
    assert 2 * x + 2 * y + 2 * z == 6
    assert x - y == 0

x, y, z = sol(1)
print(x)
print(y)
print(z)

traps: Dividing by a zero pivot instead of swapping in a lower row first. The swap is legal and costs nothing; the division is undefined.
Treating a column with no pivot as if it had one. A skipped column means a free variable, not a missing equation.
Using the first row's multiplier on the wrong row: R_i ← R_i − m·R_k zeroes a_ik only when m = a_ik / a_kk taken from the current matrix, not from the original one.
Forgetting that a zero row [0 0 0 | 0] carries no information, while [0 0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0 means no solution at all.
Sign slips in back substitution: y + z/2 = 3/2 gives y = (3 − t)/2, but multiplying only the left side by 2 gives a wrong answer.

quiz.q: Define pivot and multiplier in Gaussian elimination.
quiz.a: The pivot is the first non-zero entry of a row after elimination, used to clear its column. The multiplier is m = a_ik / a_kk, the factor that makes entry a_ik below the pivot become zero.

quiz.q: State the two properties of reduced row echelon form.
quiz.a: Every pivot equals 1, and every pivot is the only non-zero entry in its column; zeros lie below and above pivots, and rows of zeros sit at the bottom.

quiz.q: Why does Gauss–Jordan need no back substitution?
quiz.a: It clears the entries above each pivot as well as below, then scales pivots to 1. The pivot columns become unit columns, so each pivot row reads x_k = b′_k directly.

quiz.q: Why is a skipped pivot column linked to a free variable?
quiz.a: No pivot means no equation fixes that unknown as a leading variable, so it can be chosen freely and the pivot unknowns are then expressed in terms of it.

quiz.q: Use Gauss–Jordan to solve x + 2y + z = 8, 2x + y − z = 1, x − y + 2z = 5.
quiz.a: Reduction gives RREF [1 0 0 | 1], [0 1 0 | 2], [0 0 1 | 3], so x = 1, y = 2, z = 3. Check in row 2: 2(1) + 2 − 3 = 1 ✓.

quiz.q: A consistent system has 6 unknowns and 3 pivots after elimination. How many free parameters does the general solution have?
quiz.a: n − r = 6 − 3 = 3 free parameters, say t₁, t₂, t₃.

quiz.q: A student reaches an echelon form with a skipped pivot column and concludes the system has no solution. Explain the error.
quiz.a: A skipped column gives a free variable and infinitely many solutions, provided the system is consistent. No solution needs a contradictory row [0 0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0; a free variable carries no contradiction.

quiz.q: Why does choosing the largest entry in the pivot column as pivot keep the computation stable?
quiz.a: All multipliers then have |m| ≤ 1, so row updates only subtract a fraction of another row and entries do not grow. Small growth keeps rounding error small, which matters on a computer storing numbers approximately.

beyond: Not for the exam. Elimination is what every solver runs before you see an answer: LAPACK, MATLAB's backslash and NumPy's solve all perform a pivoted LU decomposition first. Numerical analysts study the growth factor, how large entries become during elimination, because it decides whether the printed digits can be trusted. Sparse variants handle circuit and power-grid systems with millions of rows by skipping structural zeros. Least squares in Unit 5 is built on the same reduction. Search 'partial pivoting', 'growth factor' and 'sparse Gaussian elimination' to go further.
